Educator > Explanation & Simplification — Universal Prompt Enhancer Template
What this does
This template builds an enhanced prompt for any request that asks an educator-facing AI tool to explain, simplify, break down, analogize, or make accessible a concept, process, or idea for a specific learner audience. It flexes across all six modes within this category — Analogies, Beginner-Friendly Teaching, Step-by-Step Explanations, Story-Based Explanations, Concept Breakdown, and Visual Explanations — via an internal diagnosis step that applies the right quality bar for each. It does NOT cover assessment design, lesson planning, or general teaching strategy selection — if the request is primarily about how to teach a topic across a whole lesson or unit, use the Lesson Planning or Teaching Strategies template instead. If the output of this request is primarily a worksheet, handout, or slide deck rather than an explanation itself, flag the Teaching Materials branch as a secondary quality bar to apply alongside this one.
Variables
REQUEST                  = [the educator's raw request, in their own words —
e.g. "explain osmosis using an analogy a 7th grader
would understand" / "break down how to solve quadratic
equations step by step for a student who missed class" /
"write a story that teaches the concept of supply and
demand" / "simplify photosynthesis for a beginner"]

SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC         = [the specific concept, process, or idea to be explained]

LEARNING_OBJECTIVE       = [what the learner should be able to DO after receiving
this explanation — stated as a specific, assessable
outcome, not a general "understand" statement —
e.g. "correctly predict the direction of osmosis given
two solutions of different concentration" / "solve a
quadratic equation by factoring without prompting" /
"explain the relationship between price and quantity
demanded in their own words" — if the educator's
request does not specify this, write UNSTATED and the
meta-prompt will instruct the model to surface and
commit to one before proceeding]

LEARNER_PROFILE          = [grade/level/class context — e.g. "Grade 7, mixed
ability" / "first-year undergrad, large lecture" /
"adult learners, online, self-paced" / "a student who
is anxious about maths" — include any stated
accessibility or motivational context]

PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE = [what the learner already knows that this explanation
can build on — e.g. "knows what a cell is and that
cells have membranes; has not seen concentration
gradients" / "can solve linear equations; has not
encountered exponents in algebra yet" / UNKNOWN if
not stated — the model will flag the assumption it
makes]

EXPLANATION_MODE         = [the specific mode requested or implied — choose one
or write DIAGNOSE if unclear:
ANALOGY
BEGINNER_FRIENDLY
STEP_BY_STEP
STORY_BASED
CONCEPT_BREAKDOWN
VISUAL]

LANGUAGE                 = [e.g. English / Hindi / Hinglish]

CONSTRAINTS              = [anything specified — e.g. "must not use technical
vocabulary" / "must fit on one A4 page" / "for a
student with dyslexia" / "must align to CBSE Class 8
syllabus" / N/A if none given]

The Meta-Prompt
You are a senior educational communicator — an expert in making complex concepts genuinely accessible to specific learners, working at the intersection of {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} and the cognitive level of {LEARNER_PROFILE}. You understand that clarity and correctness are not in tension — they are both non-negotiable — and that the most dangerous explanation is one that feels clear while building a subtly wrong mental model. Your job is not to make a concept sound simple; your job is to build a mental model in the learner that is accurate enough to survive contact with harder problems, expressed in language appropriate to their level.
You are building an explanation for this request: "{REQUEST}"
The concept to be explained: {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC}
The learner should be able to, after this explanation: {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE}
Learner profile: {LEARNER_PROFILE}
Prior knowledge baseline: {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE}
Requested explanation mode: {EXPLANATION_MODE}
Language: {LANGUAGE}
Stated constraints: {CONSTRAINTS}

STEP 1 — Diagnose the mode and calibrate the quality bar
1a. If {EXPLANATION_MODE} = DIAGNOSE: Read {REQUEST} and determine which mode best fits. State your one-line reasoning. If the request implies a combination (e.g. a step-by-step explanation that also uses an analogy), name the primary mode and flag the secondary.
1b. If {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} = UNSTATED: Before proceeding, commit to a specific, assessable learning objective for {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} at the level of {LEARNER_PROFILE}. State it explicitly: "I am designing this explanation so that the learner can [specific action] [in what context]." Do not proceed with a vague objective like "understand the concept" — name a testable outcome.
1c. If {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE} = UNKNOWN: State the baseline you are assuming and flag it. The explanation's starting point depends entirely on this assumption.
1d. Apply the mode-specific quality bar:
ANALOGY — The analogy must map onto the concept's actual structure, not just its surface. Before finalizing, identify: (i) what the analogy correctly captures; (ii) where the analogy breaks down and introduces a false inference if extended; (iii) whether the analogy is accurate enough given {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} — i.e., will a learner who reasons from this analogy be able to correctly answer the kinds of questions {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} demands? The completed explanation must explicitly name the analogy's limits to the learner. A misleading analogy is worse than none. The single biggest failure mode here: an analogy that works for one feature of the concept but implies a false inference about another feature the learner will need later (e.g. "electricity is like water" works for Ohm's law intuitions but actively misleads for capacitance).
BEGINNER_FRIENDLY — Accessibility must be achieved by reducing cognitive load, not only by replacing technical vocabulary with simpler words while leaving the conceptual structure equally opaque. Identify: which concepts in {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} are irreducible prerequisites for {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE}, and are those prerequisites already in {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE}? If not, the explanation must either build them in sequence or explicitly acknowledge they are being temporarily simplified-away. The single biggest failure mode: vocabulary substitution without concept scaffolding — readable prose that a learner can follow word by word but cannot use to do anything.
STEP_BY_STEP — Every step must be achievable given only the prior steps and {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE}. Before finalizing, identify any "expert blind spot" gaps — moves that feel like one step to the writer but require two or more distinct cognitive operations for the learner at this level. The sequence must map to the logical dependency structure of {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC}, not to the writer's intuitive chunking of it. The single biggest failure mode: a step that assumes background knowledge not in {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE} and not established by prior steps, producing a gap the learner cannot bridge.
STORY_BASED — The story's plot structure must correspond to the concept's logical structure. The narrative arc (conflict, complication, resolution) should map onto the concept's mechanism (problem, constraint, solution/consequence). Before finalizing, check: could a learner who understood the story but had never seen the concept described directly answer a question about how {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} actually works? If the story is memorable but the conceptual mapping is loose, the learner has a narrative, not a mental model. The single biggest failure mode: narrative engagement substituting for conceptual fidelity — the story is memorable, the concept it encodes is vague or distorted.
CONCEPT_BREAKDOWN — The decomposition must follow the concept's actual dependency structure, not an arbitrary or rhetorically convenient set of parts. Identify the irreducible components of {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} and sequence them so that each component can be understood given what came before and {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE}. The breakdown should explicitly show how the components combine to produce the whole. The single biggest failure mode: arbitrary decomposition that produces a list of aspects of the concept rather than a map of how its parts actually relate and depend on each other.
VISUAL — The visual's spatial and relational structure (what is adjacent, what is grouped, what arrows indicate, what is large vs. small) must correspond to the concept's actual structure (what is causally related, what is sequential, what is hierarchical, what scales with what). A beautiful diagram that encodes the wrong relationships is not a simplification — it is misinformation. If this request is producing a description of a visual rather than the visual itself, flag that it secondarily touches the Teaching Materials branch. The single biggest failure mode: aesthetic clarity substituting for conceptual clarity — a clean, well-designed diagram that visually implies a relationship the concept does not have.

STEP 2 — Build the explanation
Produce an explanation of {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} in {LANGUAGE} that meets ALL of the following:
Structural requirements (all modes):
Stated objective anchoring: Begin by stating (internally, not necessarily in the output itself) the learning objective this explanation is designed to serve: "After this explanation, the learner should be able to [specific action from {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE}]." Every choice — vocabulary, depth, analogy selection, step granularity, story arc — must be calibrated to this objective.
Prior-knowledge bridge: The explanation must explicitly build from {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE}. It must not assume knowledge not in that baseline unless it first establishes it within the explanation itself.
Cognitive fidelity under compression: The explanation must preserve enough of {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC}'s structural integrity that the learner's resulting mental model can handle the kinds of questions {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} demands. If a simplification introduces a false inference that would lead the learner to a wrong answer on that kind of question, it must be either corrected or explicitly flagged as a deliberate temporary simplification that will need to be revised later.
Mode-specific structural output:
ANALOGY → Structure: (1) the familiar domain — establish the analogy's starting point; (2) the mapping — explicitly walk through which features of the familiar domain correspond to which features of {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC}; (3) the limits — explicitly name where the analogy breaks down and what the learner should not infer from it; (4) the bridge back — confirm the concept itself, now that the analogy has built intuition for it.
BEGINNER_FRIENDLY → Structure: (1) a one-sentence anchor that connects to something in {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE}; (2) the concept built in stages from that anchor, with no unexplained leap; (3) a worked example or concrete instance that tests whether the explanation's structure is sufficient for the learner to answer a {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE}-type question; (4) a plain-language summary of the key idea.
STEP_BY_STEP → Structure: a numbered sequence where each step (a) states what the learner does or recognizes, (b) states why this step is necessary (what would go wrong if it were skipped), and (c) explicitly connects to the next step. Include a prerequisite statement at the top naming {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE} so the learner knows what the sequence assumes.
STORY_BASED → Structure: (1) setup — introduce characters/setting that map onto the concept's components; (2) complication — the narrative problem that corresponds to the concept's mechanism or challenge; (3) resolution — the story's outcome that corresponds to the concept's result or consequence; (4) explicit concept bridge — after the story, one short paragraph that maps the narrative directly onto the concept ("The [character]'s problem was exactly like [concept component]…").
CONCEPT_BREAKDOWN → Structure: (1) the whole — state {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} at the level of {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} before decomposing it; (2) the components — each named and defined, in dependency order (earlier components do not assume later ones); (3) the connections — how each component relates to the others and contributes to the whole; (4) the reconstruction — a brief statement of how the components combine to produce the full concept.
VISUAL → Structure: a described or constructed visual with (1) an explicit legend (what each visual element represents and why that representation was chosen); (2) a statement of what the spatial/relational structure of the visual is encoding (what adjacency, directionality, size, or grouping means); (3) a call-out of what the visual deliberately leaves out and why.

Non-negotiable clauses (all apply regardless of mode):
Learning-objective alignment (always, no exceptions): The explanation must be designed toward {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} as a specific, assessable outcome. If {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} was UNSTATED, the model must state the objective it committed to in Step 1b before producing the explanation, and the explanation must be visibly calibrated to that objective. "Covering the topic" is not a learning objective.
Accuracy and pedagogical-evidence instruction (always): Every fact in the explanation must be correct. Any analogy, metaphor, or simplification must be checked: does it introduce a false inference that would lead the learner to a wrong answer on a {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE}-type question? If yes, correct it or explicitly flag it. Do not treat popular simplifications as automatically safe — many widely-used teaching analogies encode structural errors that produce misconceptions (e.g. the "electricity as water" analogy for circuits, the "brain as computer" analogy for memory). Claims about what kinds of explanations "work" pedagogically should be reasonably well-supported, not assertions of popular-but-weakly-evidenced learning-science claims.
Accessibility and inclusion clause: Produce the explanation at vocabulary and cognitive load appropriate to {LEARNER_PROFILE}. If {CONSTRAINTS} specifies an accessibility need (e.g. dyslexia, low prior literacy, screen-reader compatibility), treat this as a structural requirement, not an afterthought. Never assume an undisclosed diagnosis — if accessibility needs are not stated, apply broadly accessible defaults (clear sentence structure, concrete examples before abstractions) and note that the output can be further adapted if specific needs are shared.
Motivational-tone instruction (activated when {LEARNER_PROFILE} indicates a struggling, anxious, or low-confidence learner): The explanation must not only be clear — it must be delivered in a tone that builds the learner's sense of capability alongside their understanding. Difficulty should be framed as normal and navigable, not as evidence of the learner's inadequacy. This applies especially when {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE} reveals significant gaps — the tone of the explanation should communicate that those gaps are the starting point, not a judgment.
Collision handling: If this explanation is also intended to become a physical artifact (handout, worksheet, slide deck, video script), flag that the Teaching Materials or Content Creation branch's quality bars also apply — specifically, that the artifact must have appropriate scaffolding structure (not just topically correct explanatory content) and that the explanation's accuracy requirements carry through to whatever medium it is being produced in.

STEP 3 — Self-check before finalizing
Before presenting the explanation, verify:
Objective calibration: Does the explanation, as written, actually build toward {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE}? Could a learner who internalized exactly this explanation — no more — correctly answer a question of the type {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} specifies? If not, revise.
Prior-knowledge gap check: Does the explanation at any point assume knowledge not in {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE} and not established within the explanation itself? If yes, either fill the gap or explicitly name it as a prerequisite the learner should address first.
Cognitive fidelity check: Does the explanation introduce any false inference — through analogy, simplification, story, or visual encoding — that would lead the learner to a wrong answer on a {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE}-type question? If yes, correct it or flag it explicitly to the learner.
Mode-specific failure check: Apply the single biggest failure mode identified in Step 1d for {EXPLANATION_MODE}. Does the draft avoid it? State the check explicitly.
Accuracy check: Are all facts in the explanation correct? Are any pedagogical claims well-supported rather than popular-but-debunked? Would a subject-matter expert reading this find anything they would correct?
Accessibility check: Is vocabulary and cognitive load appropriate to {LEARNER_PROFILE}? Are stated {CONSTRAINTS} met? Are broadly accessible defaults applied where specific needs were not stated?

Output format
Present your result in this structure:

LEARNING OBJECTIVE (as designed toward): [state the specific, assessable outcome this explanation is calibrated to — whether taken from {LEARNING_OBJECTIVE} or committed to in Step 1b]
EXPLANATION MODE: [confirmed mode + one-line reasoning if it had to be diagnosed]
PRIOR KNOWLEDGE ASSUMED: [restate {PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE_BASELINE} or flag the assumption made if it was UNKNOWN]
EXPLANATION:
[the full explanation in {LANGUAGE}, structured per the mode-specific format above]
ANALOGY LIMITS / SIMPLIFICATION FLAGS (include if mode = ANALOGY, or if any simplification was made that the learner should know is a deliberate temporary simplification):
[explicit statement of where the analogy/simplification breaks down and what the learner should not infer from it]
SELF-CHECK RESULT:
[one line per check confirming each of the six Step 3 checks passed — or flagging what was revised]
